title: API-only E2E tests miss SSR fetch errors in Server Components
context: E2E tests for Next.js app covered only API endpoints using Playwright's request fixture (e.g., POST /api/orders, GET /api/clients). No page-level tests navigated to rendered routes.
error: Server Components making fetch() calls with relative URLs (e.g., fetch('/api/clients')) threw ERR_INVALID_URL during SSR. These errors were invisible to tests because the test suite only exercised API routes, never rendering the affected pages (/clientes/[id], /configuracoes/impressoras, /configuracoes/filamentos).
correction: Fixed all Server Component fetch calls to use full URLs with baseUrl. Converted pages with onClick handlers to 'use client' components. Root cause was that Next.js Server Components run on the server where relative URLs are invalid, but tests never triggered the SSR of those pages.
prevention: Every E2E test suite must include page-level tests that navigate to and render actual routes, not just API endpoint tests. Rule: for each page with server-side data fetching, write at least one page.goto() test that verifies the page renders without server errors. Monitor browser console for ERR_INVALID_URL during test runs.

title: E2E tests that only assert element presence miss broken navigation links
context: E2E test in page-clientes.spec.ts verified the 'Novo Cliente' button was visible using toBeVisible(), but never clicked it. The button linked to /clientes/novo which did not exist as a route, resulting in a 404 that went undetected.
error: A navigation link (/clientes/novo) was broken (404) for an unknown period. The existing E2E test only asserted the link element was visible on the page, but did not follow the link or verify the destination page rendered correctly.
correction: Created the missing route at /clientes/novo/page.tsx using the existing ClientForm component. Added a new E2E test that clicks the 'Novo Cliente' link, waits for the /clientes/novo URL, and asserts the form renders with the expected heading and submit button.
prevention: Rule: for every navigation link or button that triggers a route change, the E2E test must click it and verify the destination page renders — not just assert the element is visible. Pattern: click link → waitForURL → assert destination content. Apply this to all action buttons (Novo Cliente, Novo Pedido, Editar, etc.).

title: Over-spawning subagents burns ~15x tokens without quality gain
context: Anthropic's multi-agent research system reported 90.2% quality improvement over single-agent baseline, but burned roughly 15x the tokens of a normal chat turn. Early versions would over-spawn — firing off far more subagents than a simple question needed.
error: The orchestrator or architect spawns too many parallel subagents for the task complexity. Each fork costs ~15x tokens. When a task needs 5 researchers, they should be batched, not spawned as 5 parallel subagents.
correction: Cap parallel subagent spawning. Batch parallel work when possible. Only spawn separate subagents when each has a genuinely different role (different model, different toolset, read-only reviewer).
prevention: Every node in a graph must earn its keep: the job must genuinely have separable parts. If you can collapse your nodes back into one agent's loop and lose nothing, you should. Add a max_parallel_tokens budget that calculates: n_agents × agent_context_limit ≤ total_budget.

title: A graph of weak nodes is slop produced in parallel
context: Teams that spent early 2026 getting good at running one agent in a loop are hitting the wall where one loop is the wrong shape, and splitting work into coordinated specialized nodes. But if the nodes are weak agents, wiring them into an org chart gives you a weak org.
error: Sub-agent nodes that haven't been validated as competent are delegated graph work. Each node is only as good as the loop running inside it — discover, plan, execute, verify. A graph of shaky loops multiplies the shakiness.
correction: Nail the single loop first. Each subagent node must be a loop that reliably ships on its own. Validate that the skill for a stage has capability documentation before allowing execution.
prevention: Before wiring agents into a graph, master the loop: one agent, a clear verifier, an explicit stop condition. Get that solid and the subagents you wire together are each worth wiring. Add stage capability validation in the init phase.

title: State drift is the #1 way graphs rot
context: When wiring agents into a graph, shared state is what turns a pile of agents into a system instead of a group chat that forgets everything. State drift is the #1 way graphs rot.
error: The state.json flows between stages but there is no schema that defines which stage can write which field. Without explicit state design, stages mutate each other's data causing silent corruption.
correction: Design the shared state object explicitly. Decide what travels along the edges and who's allowed to write to it. The sub-agent contract must define immutable vs mutable fields per stage.
prevention: Every edge in the graph must carry a well-defined state contract. State that drifts is the fastest path to a broken graph. In the sub-agent contract, specify which fields each stage may write and which are read-only.

title: Knowledge graphs and agent graphs are unrelated despite shared name
context: A viral misattribution claimed Google released a free graph engineering course. The real course (DeepLearning.AI's Agentic Knowledge Graph Construction) uses Google's ADK but teaches knowledge graphs — data structures storing facts as entities and relationships — not agent graphs.
error: Confusing knowledge graphs (data, entities, relationships for retrieval) with agent graphs (execution, nodes, edges, routing). The Graphify tool is a knowledge graph. The pipeline is an agent graph. Same word, unrelated problem.
correction: Distinguish clearly in documentation. Graphify = knowledge graph (data mapping). The orchestrator pipeline = agent graph (execution orchestration). Never conflate them.
prevention: When documenting or referencing graph concepts, explicitly label whether it's knowledge-graph (data) or agent-graph (execution). The core mistake that leads to over-engineering is confusing the two.
